news.title: I started this experiment for a slightly different reason. I was playing with a system tha…
news.author: hackaday@www.urbanmind.net
news.snippet: I started this experiment for a slightly different reason. I was playing with a system that could reconstruct context across documents. Not summarize documents. Not retrieve the most similar chunks. Reconstruct context. For example, suppose I have two documents: In 2022, the team chose PostgreSQL. And somewhere else: After the migration problems, the team moved to DynamoDB in 2024. Neither document contains the answer to: Why did the database decision change? The answer lives in the relationship between them. That got me thinking about something else. If a system can reliably recover these relationships, could it also use them to create structured training data? Before going there, I wanted to know whether the relationships actually mattered. So I built a small experiment. And the first result was much stronger than I expected. I wanted to remove retrieval from the equation The obvious problem with testing relationships in RAG is retrieval. If the experiment gets better answers after adding a graph, what actually improved? Maybe the graph found documents that retrieval missed. Maybe it simply retrieved more useful evidence. Maybe the model got more context. Maybe the graph structure itself helped. Those are very different explanations. I wanted to isolate one of them. So I made the retrieved documents identical in both conditions. No re-ranking. No additional documents. No better retrieval. The model gets the same documents. The only difference is whether it also receives explicit relationships between those documents. That became the experiment: Does explicitly stated relational context improve reasoning when retrieval is held constant? The dataset I built a synthetic corpus of 254 business documents. The documents cover things like billing, DevOps and HR. Then I created 60 multi-hop cases with manually defined ground truth: 42 supersession cases 6 contradiction cases 4 negative cases 8 link cases Some cases require reasoning across several documents. Six of the supersession cases involve four to six documents with unrelated distractors. I deliberately made some of the relationships hard to recover from individual documents. For example, two documents can both be perfectly valid while representing different states of the same decision. The important information isn't inside either document. It's in: A → superseded by → B or: A ↔ contradicts ↔ B or: A → belongs to → cluster B There is also a meaningful negative case: A → no known relation → B That one turned out to matter more than I expected. The baseline was deliberately weak I used a lexical BM25-style top-5 retrieval over the full corpus. It isn't a production BM25 implementation. It's a deliberately simple lexical baseline. Mean recall of the oracle documents in the top five was 0.67. 27 of the 60 cases had full recall. 17 had partial recall. 10 had low recall. Six had zero recall, all of them negative cases. This is a real limitation. If retrieval misses evidence, a relational hint can potentially compensate for that weakness. So I don't want to pretend this experiment answers what happens with a very strong production retrieval system. But it gives us something useful: C and D see byte-identical retrieved documents . That part is controlled. Then I added the relationships The baseline looks roughly like this: retrieved documents ↓ LLM ↓ answer The experimental condition adds a small structured block: retrieved documents + explicit relationships ↓ LLM ↓ answer For example: kind: superseded from: database-choice-2022.md to: database-choice-2024.md reason: migration failure The model was told that the knowledge-base engine had detected the relation and that it should use the hint if it was consistent with the documents. Nothing else changed. The result I ran the main experiment with two models. ModelNo relationTyped relationsDeepSeek77%94%GPT-4o-mini77%98% The gain was: +17 percentage points for DeepSeek. +21 points for GPT-4o-mini. That was enough to make me stop and ask a more annoying question: What exactly did I measure? Because “adding a graph improves RAG” would be a very easy conclusion. And probably a premature one. Maybe the model just likes extra tokens The relation hints were only around 17 words. Perhaps the model simply benefited from getting more information. So I added a control with approximately the same amount of unrelated text. Parking. Cafeteria. Meeting rooms. No relation labels. No document names. No similarity scores. That condition scored 53%. The baseline was 77%. The relational condition was 98%. So “more tokens” doesn't explain the result. At least not by itself. Maybe structure is the trick The relational information was presented as fields: kind: from: to: reason: Maybe that formatting alone makes the model perform better. So I took the same semantic information and put it into ordinary prose. Something like: Note: B reflects the current state of this decision. A is the previous version. Same information. No structured relation fields. That scored 53%. The structured version scored 98%. This result bothered me. Because now I had learned something I hadn't originally set out to test: how the relationship is presented may matter almost as much as the relationship itself. And I had a new confound. Maybe the model doesn't actually reason over the relationship. Maybe it just trusts the block because I told it that a “knowledge base engine” generated it. I'll come back to that. What if the relations are wrong? This was the test I cared about most. If relationships really carry useful information, incorrect relationships should matter. I corrupted the identifying fields of the relation hints. At 20% corruption, accuracy dropped from 98% to 53%. At 40%, it was 52%. That is a dramatic failure. But there is an important detail here. I did not test every corruption level. I don't know what happens at 5%. I don't know what happens at 10%. I don't know whether another corruption mechanism would behave differently. So I can't say: “80% correct relations are useless.” The experiment doesn't show that. It shows something narrower: Under this particular corruption mechanism, introducing 20% incorrect relations almost completely destroyed the observed benefit. That distinction matters. Then I tried similarity instead of typed relationships This was probably the most interesting part of the experiment. If relationships help because they connect documents, perhaps we don't need explicit relation types. Maybe a similarity graph is enough. So I created another condition where the model received document-to-document similarity edges instead of typed relations. The result improved substantially: ModelNo hintSimilarityTyped relationDeepSeek76%88%96%GPT-4o-mini76%93%98% Similarity clearly helped. But it didn't behave like typed relations. There was a particularly interesting case. For DeepSeek, similarity actually beat typed relations on the link cases: 79% vs 71%. The likely explanation is still only a hypothesis. The typed hint contained a reason field that may have distracted the model. The negative cases were different. Similarity hurt them. The model saw related-looking documents and tended to assume that a relationship existed. The typed relation could explicitly say: kind: none That distinction matters. Similarity says: These things look related. A typed relation can say: These things are related in this specific way. Or: These things are not related. Those are different pieces of information. Then I tried to break the whole thing I added three more controls: Shuffled relations Give each case a relation from another case of the same kind. Token-matched text Give the model unrelated text with approximately the same length as the relation hint. In-document prose Put the same semantic relation into ordinary document text. All three landed around 52–53%. The baseline was 77%. The structured, correct relation condition was 98%. The shuffled condition also passed an anti-leakage check: none of the 60 shuffled hints happened to be correct. At this point I was reasonably confident that the result wasn't just: “Give the LLM some extra words that look vaguely useful.” But I still wasn't confident about why the structured relation worked. The uncomfortable explanation There is one explanation my controls don't eliminate. Maybe the model isn't using the relational structure as relational structure. Maybe it sees: Retineo relation: kind=superseded ... and interprets that as privileged metadata. In other words: “The system says this is the answer, so I'll trust it.” That would produce a large improvement without requiring the model to reconstruct anything from the relationship itself. The in-document prose control actually makes this possibility more interesting. The two conditions contain the same semantic information. Yet the structured version was dramatically more effective. So I can't currently separate: relational reasoning from authority/salience effects caused by the representation. That's the next control I want to run. There is another problem: retrieval My retrieval baseline is weak. That's not an incidental detail. Mean top-5 recall was only 0.67, so there is plenty of room for a relational hint to compensate for retrieval failures. Imagine that the model needs documents A, B and C. The retriever returns A and B. Then I give it a relation saying: A → related_to → C I haven't really solved the retrieval problem. I've given the model a shortcut around it. So the next experiment is becoming pretty obvious. I want to vary retrieval depth while keeping the relational condition intact. Something like: shallow retrieval × no relation / relation then: deeper retrieval × no relation / relation The question is not whether deeper retrieval improves the baseline. Of course it can. The interesting question is what happens to the gap between the two conditions. If: +21 pp ↓ +10 pp ↓ +2 pp then the relational hint may mostly be compensating for weak retrieval. If the gap remains large as retrieval quality improves, the story gets more interesting. But this experiment needs some care. Simply dumping 100 documents into the context changes the amount of text the model has to process, so that would introduce another variable. I want to separate more available evidence from more text in the prompt . What I think the experiment says so far Here is the version I'm comfortable with. On this synthetic corpus, with this retrieval setup and these two models: Correct typed cross-document relations improved accuracy when the retrieved documents were identical. The effect survived controls for extra tokens, shuffled relations, and expressing the same semantic information as ordinary document prose. Similarity structure also helped, but typed relations provided additional information in several cases, particularly where relation type or explicit absence mattered. That's the observation. The explanation is still open. I don't know yet how much of the effect comes from: information about the relationship itself; making that information easier for the model to parse; the model treating structured metadata as authoritative; compensation for weak retrieval. And I definitely don't know whether the effect survives real organizational data. The corpus is synthetic. The retrieval is simplified. There are only two models. Those are real boundaries on the result, not footnotes to hide at the end. This started as a data-labeling idea There was a practical reason I ran the experiment in the first place. I was thinking about whether a context-reconstruction system could help create structured datasets. Take a collection of documents. Find candidate relationships. Classify them: supersedes contradicts belongs_to references none Then use those relationships as structured training data. That sounds useful. But it also creates a nasty circular problem. If I use the system to generate relational labels, and then use those labels to demonstrate that relational context helps models, I may just be measuring my own assumptions. So I stopped. Before thinking about dataset generation, I wanted to know whether the representation itself had a measurable effect. That led to this experiment. And now I have a better question than the one I started with. The next experiment I don't want to build a bigger graph yet. I want to try to make this result disappear. Better retrieval. More evidence. Interactive retrieval. Different models. Different relational representations. And especially an experiment that removes the “trusted metadata” explanation. If better retrieval makes the relational advantage disappear, that's useful. If it doesn't, that's useful too. Either result tells me where to look next. The interesting question is no longer: Does GraphRAG work? That's too broad to be useful. The question I'm interested in is much smaller: When an LLM already has the relevant documents, does explicitly representing the relationships between those documents give it information it cannot reliably reconstruct from the documents themselves? I don't have the final answer yet. That's exactly why I'm running the next experiment. # llm # ai # rag # machinelearning # software # coding # development # engineering # inclusive # community Does RAG Need Better Retrieval — or Better Relationships?

tele.title: Comin Asia and Nokia build sovereign AI infrastructure across Southeast Asia
tele.snippet: AI-ready data centres planned for Cambodia and Laos; Nokia partnership for regional sovereign AI infrastructure.

tele.title: Huawei expands Vietnam footprint through energy, AI, and 5G partnerships
tele.snippet: Partnerships spanning digital energy, AI, telecom infrastructure and industrial digitalization in Vietnam.

tele.title: Cellcard doubles 5G footprint to 500+ sites, targets 1,000 by end-July
tele.snippet: Cellcard CSX-listed operator: 500+ 5G BTS deployed since Jan 2026 launch; accelerating toward 1,000 sites across Phnom Penh and central region.

tele.title: Huawei and ZTE strengthen presence in Vietnam with new 5G network deal wins
tele.snippet: Huawei consortium ~$23M 5G equipment contract; Viettel targeting 20,000 new 5G base stations in 2025. 11,000+ stations deployed nationwide.

tele.title: EU warns Vietnam: Chinese 5G vendors may deter foreign investment
tele.snippet: Ericsson and Nokia on core; Huawei and ZTE winning RAN/antenna contracts. EU Commissioner Sikela: 5G is the new battlefield for trusted vendors.

tele.title: Viettel targets 98% population 5G coverage; adds 20,000 sites in 2026
tele.title_orig: Viettel hướng tới phủ sóng 5G tới 98% dân số
tele.snippet: Deputy CEO Le Quang Hieu at MWC 2026: ~30,000 5G SA sites by end-2025; planning +20,000 in 2026 for 98% coverage.

tele.title: Vietnam eyes new 5G deals with Chinese tech firms despite US warnings
tele.snippet: Mobifone in talks with Huawei; Viettel and VNPT signed 5G supply contracts with ZTE and Huawei. Ericsson and Nokia still supply core network.

tele.title: Vietnam pursues new 5G deals with China despite US warnings
tele.title_orig: Việt Nam nhắm thỏa thuận 5G mới với Trung Quốc, bất chấp cảnh báo của Mỹ
tele.snippet: BBC Vietnamese: Mobifone negotiating with Huawei; Viettel/VNPT already signed with ZTE and Huawei for 5G equipment.

tele.title: Despite US warnings, Vietnam plans more 5G contracts with Chinese vendors
tele.title_orig: 不顾美国警告 越南拟与中企签更多5G网络合约
tele.snippet: Zaobao: Mobifone tender favors Chinese firms; Huawei 5G gear seen near US Consulate in HCMC; follows Viettel/VNPT ZTE/Huawei deals.

tele.title: Viettel to trial 6G in 2028 with Qualcomm strategic alliance
tele.title_orig: Viettel sẽ thử nghiệm 6G vào năm 2028
tele.snippet: MWC 2026: Viettel joins Qualcomm 6G alliance; commercial 6G target from 2029; co-develop premium AI smartphones.

tele.title: Cambodia 5G trial: Cellcard leads download speeds in early Ookla tests
tele.title_orig: អ៊ីនធើណិត 5G សាកល្បងជំហានដំបូងនៅកម្ពុជា
tele.snippet: AMS Khmer: Ookla trial shows Cellcard 548 Mbps, Smart 336 Mbps, Metfone 218 Mbps; 1,500+ 5G sites by March 2026.

tele.title: 1,500 5G base stations deployed in Cambodia's 5G race so far
tele.snippet: Smart Axiata 674, Metfone (Viettel) 531, Cellcard 289 stations. Ministry accelerating mobile and FWA rollout.

tele.title: Vietnam 5G median speed tops 500 Mbps for the first time; Viettel leads at 617 Mbps
tele.title_orig: Mạng 5G Việt Nam lần đầu vượt 500 Mbps
tele.snippet: VNNIC i-Speed Jan 2026: national 5G median 594.81 Mbps; Viettel 617 Mbps vs VNPT 311 Mbps and MobiFone 188 Mbps.

tele.title: Cambodia launches 5G as all three mobile operators switch on networks
tele.snippet: Cellcard, Metfone and Smart launched 5G from Jan 2026. Phased rollout from Phnom Penh and 14 provinces.

tele.title: Vietnam 5G mass deployment opens platform for app developers
tele.title_orig: 越南5G大规模部署：为应用程序开发搭建新平台
tele.snippet: VietnamPlus Chinese: Viettel 30,000 5G sites, 90% outdoor coverage; Huawei expert praises fast 5G e-commerce adoption.

tele.title: Huawei and ZTE win 5G contracts in Vietnam; Ericsson and Nokia retain core
tele.title_orig: 消息称华为中兴在越南斩获5G合同
tele.snippet: C114: Huawei $23M consortium deal; ZTE $20M+ antenna contracts; Nordic vendors on core; ~11,000 5G sites cover 26% population.
